astra.text:
Yeah, so I think the motivation was very connected to what I was saying earlier, right? We had these models that were getting increasingly capable, and we were starting to see that you could build agents that actually do useful things. And I wanted to understand what it takes to make that work in the real world. Like, when somebody is actually depending on this system to get something done, what are the problems that show up?

And customer support is a really interesting setting for that because there's a lot of language, obviously, but there's also action. You have to understand what the person wants, figure out what information you're missing, and then potentially go do something in a system. And there are constraints on what you can do, right? So it brings together a lot of these things that I've been interested in for a long time: language understanding, decision-making, interacting with an environment. That was a big part of the appeal for me.

I think the difference from academia is partly just how you define success. In research, you have a task, you have a benchmark, and you can measure progress on it. And that's valuable. But with a real user, the task isn't always neatly specified. They might explain something in a confusing way. They might change their mind halfway through. They might assume you know something that you don't know. So the agent has to figure out how to handle that whole interaction.

And then there's reliability. You can have a system that's really impressive in a few examples, but you need to understand all the places where it breaks. Maybe it understands the request perfectly but takes the wrong action. Maybe it takes the right action but tells the user something inaccurate about what happened. Or maybe it needs to ask a clarifying question before doing anything. Those are all different kinds of failures, and improving the language model alone doesn't automatically tell you how to handle all of them.

So, yeah, I think that's what makes the connection between research and building a product so interesting. You get a much more concrete sense of what is actually missing. And those can turn into really good research questions, right? How do you evaluate an agent over an entire conversation? How do you know it completed the task correctly? How does it recover when something goes wrong? For me, being able to think about those questions with real applications in mind was a big reason to do the sabbatical.

sol.text:
Yeah, so I think the decision was really driven by wanting to see what happens when you take all of these ideas about language agents and actually put them in front of real users, right? In academia, we can build WebShop or TAO-Bench and try to make the setting realistic, but it’s still a benchmark. At Sierra, the agent is interacting with an actual customer on behalf of an actual company, and it has to solve the problem correctly. That felt like a very natural next step for me, because it’s exactly this idea that language shouldn’t exist in isolation—the model has to understand what the user wants, use tools, take actions, and operate within the rules of the business.

And I think the problems become quite different once you’re in that environment. At Princeton, you can isolate a research question and measure progress on a clean dataset. In production, everything is messy. Users are ambiguous, the tools can fail, the underlying state can change, and there are many different objectives. You want the customer to be happy, but you also need the agent to follow policy, avoid incorrect actions, and know when it should ask for clarification or hand things off. And because these interactions can have real consequences, being correct most of the time is not really sufficient—the failures matter enormously.

So for me, Sierra was a chance to learn what the real bottlenecks are. You very quickly discover that getting a model to produce an impressive response is only one part of the problem. Reliability, evaluation, tool use, controllability, and understanding these long, multi-turn interactions are all equally important. That experience also fed back into the research questions I care about: how do we evaluate agents realistically, how do we make them robust, and eventually how do we improve them from interaction and feedback? It was a very complementary experience to Princeton, and honestly a lot of fun because the research loop is so immediate—you build something, deploy it, and very quickly learn where your assumptions were wrong.

opus.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is a lot of it was timing. Like, this was right around when, you know, we had done WebShop, we'd done ReAct, and all of these things were sort of working in the lab, right? And you could see that there was this, like, gap opening up between what we were writing papers about and what was actually about to get deployed in front of real people. And I just felt like if I stayed purely on the academic side, I would be guessing at what the real problems were. And I don't like guessing, right? I'd rather go and see it.

And then the other part was just the people. Like, I knew Bret and Clay, and I think when you're evaluating something like this, honestly the team matters way more than the idea. Because the idea's gonna change six times anyway. So that part was, was pretty easy for me.

But I think the thing that was genuinely eye-opening — and I tell my students this all the time now — is that in academia, if you build an agent that works 60% of the time on some benchmark, and the previous number was 45, that's a great paper, right? Like, that's a fantastic paper. In production, 60% is, is unusable. It's worse than unusable, because now you have a system that's confidently wrong in front of a customer who's trying to, like, cancel a flight or get a refund. So the entire, the entire framing shifts from "can it do this" to "does it do this every single time, and when it doesn't, does it fail in a way that's safe?" And that tail, that last chunk, is like 90% of the work. Nobody writes papers about that.

The second thing, which is I think the one that really got me, is evaluation. Because in research, evaluation is, is kind of a solved problem in the sense that you have a test set, you have a metric, you run it, you get a number. In the real world there's no ground truth, right? You have a customer who has a 40-page policy document, and the agent has to follow that policy, and you need to know if it did. And that's, like, genuinely hard. That's a research problem. And that's actually literally where TAO-Bench came from. Like, TAO-Bench is just us taking the shape of the problems we were staring at every day and turning it into something the community could work on.

And then the third thing, which I didn't appreciate before, is that a lot of what you want from these agents is not intelligence, it's compliance. Like, the model is smart enough. The question is, will it do the boring thing you told it to do, consistently, when it thinks it has a better idea? And those are, those are actually kind of opposing pressures.

So yeah, I came back to Princeton with, like, a whole list of problems I would never have come up with sitting in my office. Which was, which was really the point.

Let’s put them in more realistic settings. And at some point you realize even those benchmarks, the ceiling is still pretty low compared to what the models can actually do, and compared to what people actually need.

So the conviction for me was, okay, these models had finally gotten to a point where that was even possible. When I was at OpenAI back then, it was a nonprofit, a very well-funded research lab, super fun, lots of ideas floating around — multi-agent stuff, RL, robotics, Dota, GPT. But you weren’t deploying agents that talk to real customers every day. The models just weren’t there. Best thing we had before GPT was an LSTM that writes one sentence and goes off the rails. Suddenly now you can actually build a company around this, and it was working. That was pretty compelling.

And the other piece was, I already had the faculty job, right? That was the whole reason I left OpenAI the first time — I wanted to work with students on a bunch of different directions. A sabbatical lets you go deep on the industry side without giving that up. So it wasn’t like I was choosing industry over academia the way I was in 2017. It was more like, I want to see the real version of this agent stuff up close, and then bring that back.

As for the problems that were different… I think in academia you’re often optimizing for, can I show a new capability, can I define a new task, can I write a paper that pushes the envelope. At Sierra the problems are much more about, does this actually work when a real person is on the other end, right? Reliability, consistency, the long tail of weird cases, latency, all the stuff that never shows up on a leaderboard. You can have an agent that’s 80% on some benchmark and that’s a great paper. You cannot have an agent that’s 80% with a customer and call that a product.

There’s also this evaluation problem that’s just completely different. In the lab you design the benchmark, you know the distribution. In production the distribution is whatever customers throw at you tomorrow. And that loops back to the thing I always believed, that language doesn’t exist in isolation. In an enterprise setting that’s even more true — the language is grounded in policies, tools, databases, brand voice, all of that. So a lot of the research questions become, how do you make these agents robust in that grounded setting, not just clever in a chat window.

Yeah, it was a really different set of constraints, but in a good way. It sort of forces you to be honest about what actually matters.

gemini.text:
Yeah, so Sierra was really an incredible experience. First of all, a big part of the conviction was just the team. When Bret and Clay reached out and we started talking about the vision, it just resonated so deeply with what I had been thinking about for years. I mean, we had been working on ReAct, WebShop, language agents in my lab, and around late 2022 and 2023, it was becoming super clear that agents weren't just a fun academic curiosity anymore. They were actually ready to do real work in the real world. And Bret and Clay have this incredible track record of building enterprise products at massive scale, so having that combination of world-class leadership and the right problem at the right time made it a really easy decision to take a sabbatical and join.

In terms of the problems and how they differed from Princeton—honestly, it was night and day. In academia, if you write a paper and your agent gets, say, 60% or 70% success rate on a challenging benchmark, that’s a top-tier paper, right? That’s SOTA, everyone's clapping, you publish at NeurIPS or ICML and you're happy. But in the real world, if you go to a company and say, "Hey, our agent works 70% of the time, and the other 30% it might give away free products or completely hallucinate a return policy," they'll laugh you out of the room. You just can't deploy that.

So the nature of the research problem fundamentally shifts from pushing average-case accuracy to solving the reliability and safety bottleneck. How do you get these stochastic, creative language models to follow strict business logic deterministically? How do you guarantee zero hallucinations on critical enterprise policies, while still keeping the conversational flexibility, empathy, and reasoning that makes LLMs great in the first place? And then you have all the systems challenges: latency, multi-turn state tracking over long contexts, secure integrations with messy, real-world enterprise APIs. 

It was super eye-opening. It really forced me to think about agent design not just as prompt engineering or one-off architectures, but as full-stack systems with proper guardrails, evaluation loops, and deterministic execution. It gave me a whole new appreciation for the gap between a research prototype and a production-grade agent.

kimi.text:
Yeah, so Sierra in some sense felt like a pretty natural evolution of the stuff we were doing at Princeton, right? Like, in the lab we'd been building these agents and putting out benchmarks like WebShop and SWE-Bench, and the whole question there was, okay, can these systems actually handle realistic tasks, right? And Sierra was basically doing that, but for real, like, for real enterprises, at real scale. These are agents that are actually talking to millions of end users on behalf of these large companies. So when the opportunity came along, it was kind of like, okay, here's a chance to actually close that loop, right? To see whether the stuff we've been dreaming about in research actually works when it meets the real world. And honestly I think the timing felt right too. This was around the point where it was becoming clear that these models had crossed some threshold where agents weren't just, like, a research curiosity anymore, they could actually be useful.

And I'll be honest, part of it was also just that as a professor you get the chance to take a sabbatical, right? So it felt like, okay, rather than go to another large lab, this was a chance to be at a small company where you're, like, directly close to the problem. You're talking to customers, you're seeing their actual pain points. And that combination of, like, working on very specific, very concrete problems but bringing in the latest cutting-edge research to solve them, that was really attractive to me.

In terms of the problems, I think the biggest difference compared to Princeton is reliability, right? In research you can get really excited about a system that works, like, 70, 80% of the time, and you write a paper and it's great. But when you have an agent that's representing a large brand and talking to their customers, every single failure is a real person having a bad experience, right? So you start caring a lot more about the worst case, not just the average case. You need guardrails, you need to be evaluating things continuously, you need to sort of earn the trust of these businesses over time. And a lot of the academic benchmarks we had just didn't capture any of that. There's all this latent ambiguity in real-world tasks, where the spec is never fully written down and you have to figure out what people actually want. So in a way, that experience fed directly back into the research, right? Like, things like TAO-Bench came out of thinking about, okay, how do we even measure whether an agent is good enough to be trusted in these kinds of settings?

fable.text:
Yeah, so I think, like, the Sierra decision was, like, pretty interesting, right? Because, like I said, for me one of the main threads has always been, like, okay, I want to see these things work in the real world, right? Not just in a benchmark, not just in a paper. And so around, like, 2023, right, ChatGPT had come out, everyone was excited about agents, and I kind of felt like, okay, if I really believe that these agents are gonna, like, do useful things for people, I should probably go and see what it actually takes to make that happen. Right? Because there's a big gap between, like, a demo and something that a company is actually gonna put in front of their customers.

And so, Bret and Clay, the founders, I think the thing that gave me conviction was basically twofold. One is just, like, the people, right? Bret was obviously, like, CTO at Facebook, was at Salesforce, he was on the board of OpenAI, right? Clay was at Google for a long time. So these are people who've, like, built stuff at scale, right? And they had, like, a very clear thesis that, like, hey, agents are gonna be the thing that companies interact with their customers through. It was not, like, "Oh, we'll figure it out." It was, like, very, very crisp, right? And the second thing was, like, customer support, or, like, customer experience in general, if you think about it, is actually, like, a really nice testbed, right? Because it's, like, it has all the ingredients that I care about. There's language, obviously, it's conversational, but the agent has to actually take actions. It has to, like, call APIs, look up your order, cancel something, issue a refund. And it has to follow rules, right? Like, there are policies. Like, you can't just refund everyone who asks. So it's like, it's basically, like, grounding, RL, all of that, but with, like, real stakes. And so for me, it was kind of like, oh, this is, like, the perfect place to actually, like, stress test all of these ideas.

And I think in terms of, like, the problems being different, yeah, they're very different, right? So in academia, you know, you get a benchmark, you get, like, 70%, you're like, "Great, we improved over the baseline by 10 points," you write it up, right? At Sierra, you're like, okay, this is going to talk to, like, millions of customers. If it's wrong 5% of the time, that's, like, a lot of people, right? So the whole notion of, like, reliability just becomes, like, front and center. And that's actually where a lot of the TAO-Bench stuff came from, right? Like, we realized that, hey, these models, if you run them once on a task, maybe they get it right. If you run them, like, eight times, they get it right, like, once or twice. And, like, that's not okay. Like, from a product standpoint, you need it to be right every single time, right? So this, like, whole pass^k idea, like, consistency, that came directly out of, like, sitting there and, like, looking at what's actually breaking.

And then there's just, like, a bunch of stuff that you never think about in academia, right? Like, latency. Like, nobody's gonna wait 30 seconds for the agent to think through, like, a tree of thoughts. Cost, right? Like, you can't, like, do, like, a hundred samples per query. And then, like, the messiness of the real world. Like, the user is, like, typing in the middle of a sentence, they're, like, changing their mind, the API is, like, returning some error, right? Like, none of that is in a benchmark. So I think what I took away from that, honestly, is, like, our benchmarks in academia are actually, like, too clean, right? And so a lot of what I've been trying to do since then is, like, bring some of that messiness back into the research, right? Like, how do you actually evaluate these things in a way that, like, reflects what you'd see if you deployed it? So yeah, it was a super, super useful two years. And I think it made me a better researcher, honestly, because, like, you get, like, grounded in what actually matters.
